newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Dollar to remain darling after Socialist win.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Dollar to remain darling after Socialist win.

text.p: The dollar, basking near a four-week peak against the mark and French franc in Europe, is set to remain the darling of currency markets after France's left-wing opposition Socialists swept into power, casting a fresh shadow over European monetary union's future.

"There is a lot of confusion from investors on how to read the French-election result. You can either read it as implying a weaker euro or an EMU delay. And those two different scenarios have radically different implications for financial markets," said Sally Wilkinson, senior economist at Daiwa Europe.
The dollar surged over a pfennig to four-week highs of 1.7280 marks on Monday against 1.7082/92 in late Europe on Friday. At 1230 GMT it was at 1.7273/78 marks.
Against the French franc, it jumped to near one-month peaks of 5.8302 against 5.7690/20. At 1230 GMT it stood at 5.8220/40.

"This (the election) has been the straw that has broken the camel's back, as it raises further uncertainty about European issues - particularly those concerning EMU. That is why sterling and the dollar have done well over the last 24 hours," said Ian Gunner, economist at Chase Investment Bank.

The U.S. unit is poised to remain a favourite with investors wary about a delay to EMU's start-date, slated for January 1999, and growing expectations that it will be launched with a broad-base of countries, forging a soft euro from the start.

Yield differentials for the dollar, moreover, further improve its upside potential, said analysts, even if EMU-inspired gains prop it too high against the yen, possibly promting verbal intervention from authorities.
"For the time being, of the two different scenarios the weakened euro seems to be taking precedence with investors moving out of deutschmarks and French francs," said Daiwa's Wilkinson.
The prospect of a soft euro would further weaken the German currency, but analysts say a delay to EMU would prompt investment back into the mark.

Uncertainty over how heavily Socialist leader and new Prime Minsiter Lionel Jospin will have to rely in his new government on the Communists, who have already demanded relaxing the Maastricht criteria, has also added a spanner into EMU's works.

"That the Socialists will need to rely on the parliamentary support of the Communist party will increase concerns about a market shift in political priorities and in particular a relaxation in fiscal control," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Markets are closely watching France for any signs of EMU delay after Jospin, whose party and allies won 273 seats in the new 577 member National Assembly, said voters had demanded reorientation on Europe.

He said the election is a "demand for justice, a demand for a profound renewal of our public life and democracy, a demand for an economic and social policy put at the service of man and a demand for a reorientation of European construction..."

Analysts said this probably means a softer interpretation of the Maastricht treaty's targets on inflation, budget deficits and debts, allowing countries such as Spain and Italy to join from the start. And delivering what the Socialists promised a pro-growth, pro-job platform against the fiscal austerity required to meet the Maastricht criteria.

Victory for France's Socialists comes on the heels of the German government's plans to revalue Bundesbank assets in a bid to qualify for EMU - both improving the odds of a broad-based EMU and a softer euro from the outset.

The government's plans to revalue the assets in order to meet the Maastricht criteria, is likely to strip Germany of its bargaining position and any opposition it has against Spain and Italy joining at the outset.

"It (revaluation) has weakened Germany's bargaining position within Europe in that they no longer can claim to be virtuous in regard to fiscal policy...and on that basis it gives the French and Italians a much stronger bargaining position," said Daiwa's Wilkinson.
